title: The torch held still
hookLine: a sparkler whirled in the dark draws circles that aren't there. the Karika's last section: the firebrand, held still
carry: the world is consciousness moving, like a whirled torch
tomorrow: The first hymn is to fire

lines: HELD STILL: ONE POINT OF LIGHT.
cards: A backyard after dark, and a kid with a sparkler. She swings it fast, and a ring of light hangs in the air. She writes her name, and for half a second the letters float there.
Then she holds it still. No ring. No letters.
Just one small spitting point of light at the end of a wire. The circles never existed apart from that point. They were the point, moving.
Gaudapada names the last section of the Mandukya Karika for nearly this picture, a burning stick from the fire, and today is the last day with him.

teach.b: The Karika's last section is called Alatashanti, the quieting of the firebrand. An alata is a burning stick, a torch pulled from the fire.
Gaudapada says: when a firebrand is whirled, it appears straight, or crooked, or circling. In the same way, when consciousness moves, it appears as the one who perceives and the things perceived.
When the firebrand is still, it is free of those shapes, and so is consciousness. Then he presses further.

teach.h: THE SHAPES COME FROM NOWHERE ELSE.
teach.b: When the torch moves, the circles don't come into it from somewhere else. When it stops, they don't go off somewhere else, and they don't sink back inside it either. They were never things on their own.
On his reading, the world of experience isn't a second thing standing apart from consciousness. It's how consciousness appears when it moves.
Advaita teachers often reach for this picture to explain maya: the world isn't nothing, and it isn't fake; it just isn't a second thing apart from consciousness. He knows this is hard to hear.
In this same section he speaks of a teaching that is deep and hard to see, and at the very end he salutes it, bowing as well as he is able.

teach.h: THE KARIKA ENDS WITH A BOW.
teach.b: So the Karika ends not with an argument but with a bow. Advaita teachers count him as an early voice of their lineage, and tradition says he taught the teacher of Shankara.
Other schools of Vedanta read the world as more fully real, with their own arguments.

how: In Advaita Vedanta, the Mandukya Upanishad is often studied together with Gaudapada's Karika and Shankara's commentary on both, and the firebrand image is used by teachers to point to consciousness behind the movement of the mind.

o: Gaudapada's verses that end with a still torch
a hymn sung while whirling a torch at night
the story of Shankara's own childhood teacher

p: a burning stick from the fire
a bow, as well as he is able

s: for Gaudapada, the shapes come into the torch from somewhere else
they don't come in from elsewhere, don't go elsewhere, and don't sink back inside. they were never things on their own.
the Karika ends with a salute, not an argument
he bows to a teaching he calls deep and hard to see.
Alatashanti means the lighting of the firebrand
it's the quieting of the firebrand: the torch held still.

games.q: you've spent a whole book arguing that the world is consciousness in motion. you reach the last verse. what do you do?
o: sum up the argument one more time.
bow to the truth you've been pointing at.
games.why: Gaudapada ends with a salute: he bows, as well as he is able, to a teaching he calls deep and hard to see.

practice: Watch the mind's motion, plans, pictures, bits of conversation, each one a shape the torch draws as it swings, without trying to stop any of it.

Between them, look for a moment when the swinging slows and there is simply awareness, drawing nothing, and rest there as long as it lasts. If you pray, you can end by bowing your head, the way the Karika ends.

wordCard.voice: The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, which end with a torch held still and a bow to a truth he calls deep and hard to see.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the quieting of the firebrand, from alata, a burning stick, and shanti, peace. The name of the Karika's last section.

carryVoice: Your line: the world is consciousness moving, like a whirled torch. Held still, the torch draws no circles. Tomorrow, the Vedas themselves.

sources.ref: Mandukya Karika 4.47–4.52 (the firebrand whirled appears straight or crooked; consciousness vibrating appears as perceiver and perceived; the shapes neither come from elsewhere, go elsewhere, nor enter into it)
Mandukya Karika 4.100 (the state deep and hard to see; the salute offered as well as one is able)
